1.title: AI Regulations Deep Dive
1.text: This is the longest module in the course, and the most important to get current. We're going deep on the actual rules — in three parts. Part A, the EU AI Act. Part B, the United States. And Part C, the rest of the world. Let's dig in.

1.title: A Note on Currency
1.text: Before we start, one essential caveat. AI law is moving faster than any other area of regulation right now — faster than tax, faster than privacy. So everything in this module is accurate as of mid-2026, but you should treat every specific date as "last known" rather than gospel. Two areas in particular are moving under our feet: the EU AI Act's high-risk timeline, which shifted in 2026, and the US federal-versus-state preemption fight, which is actively contested. When real decisions ride on a date, verify it against the primary source and your counsel. With that flag planted, let's begin.

1.title: Part A — The EU AI Act at a Glance
1.text: Part A: the EU AI Act. Formally, it's Regulation 2024/1689, and it's the world's first comprehensive, horizontal AI law — "horizontal" meaning it cuts across all sectors rather than regulating just one industry. It entered into force on the first of August 2024 and phases in over several years, through 2028. It's risk-based, and it's extraterritorial. This is the law the rest of the world reacts to and benchmarks against, so if you internalize one regulation from this entire course, make it this one. Everything else will feel familiar by comparison.

1.title: Scope & Key Definitions
1.text: Let's nail the scope. The Act defines an AI system, broadly, as a machine-based system that infers, from the inputs it receives, how to generate outputs — predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions. That definition is deliberately wide. On roles: it distinguishes providers and deployers, who carry different duties, and it also reaches importers and distributors. And critically, it's extraterritorial: it applies if the system is placed on the EU market, or if the system's output is used in the EU — no matter where your company sits. So two things decide whether the Act applies to you and what you owe: who you are in the chain, and whether there's an EU nexus. Not your headquarters.

1.title: The Risk Pyramid
1.text: The heart of the Act is the risk pyramid — four tiers. At the top, unacceptable risk: these uses are prohibited outright. Next, high-risk: permitted, but only with a strict set of obligations. Then limited risk: mainly transparency duties — for instance, telling people they're talking to a bot or labeling a deepfake. And at the base, minimal risk: no specific obligations, which covers the vast majority of AI — your spam filter, the AI in a video game. The principle is that obligations scale with risk. And notice where the weight sits: almost all the compliance burden is in the top two tiers. So your single most consequential step is classifying a system into the correct tier.

1.title: Tier 1 — Prohibited Practices (Article 5)
1.text: Let's go tier by tier, starting at the top: the prohibited practices in Article 5. Eight categories are simply banned in the EU. Subliminal or manipulative techniques that cause harm. Exploiting the vulnerabilities of people because of their age or disability. Social scoring. Predictive policing based solely on profiling someone. Untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases. Emotion recognition in workplaces and schools. Biometric categorization that sorts people by sensitive traits like race or political opinion. And real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces by law enforcement, with only narrow exceptions. These have been enforceable since February 2025. And as of December 2026, two more are added: AI tools that generate non-consensual intimate imagery, and AI-generated child sexual abuse material. The common thread: manipulation, mass surveillance, and social control.

1.title: Tier 2 — High-Risk Systems (Annex III)
1.text: The tier where most of the real governance work happens is high-risk, and it's defined in two ways. Annex III lists eight sensitive domains: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services like credit and insurance and benefits, law enforcement, migration and border control, and the administration of justice and democratic processes. Separately, Annex I covers AI that acts as a safety component of an already-regulated product — think medical devices, machinery, vehicles. For our purposes, look at that fourth Annex III domain: employment. That's where Helios's hiring tool lives, and it's why that tool carries the heaviest set of obligations in the whole Act.

1.title: High-Risk Obligations — The Checklist
1.text: So what does a high-risk system actually have to do? Here's the checklist. A risk management system. Data governance — ensuring training data is high-quality and representative. Technical documentation. Automatic logging and record-keeping. Transparency and clear instructions for deployers. Human oversight, designed into the system. Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity. An overarching quality management system. A conformity assessment, leading to CE marking. And registration in an EU database. Providers carry most of this; deployers must use the system as instructed, ensure the human oversight actually happens, and monitor it. Now look at that list again, because here's the punchline: it basically is an AI governance program. Which is why the law and good practice converge — build the program well and you've largely met the legal requirement.

1.title: GPAI & Foundation-Model Rules
1.text: The Act also regulates the model layer directly — general-purpose AI, or GPAI, the foundation models that sit beneath everyone's applications. There are two tiers here. Every GPAI provider must keep technical documentation, give information to the downstream companies that build on the model, have a copyright policy, and publish a summary of the content used to train the model. And then GPAI models deemed to carry systemic risk — the most capable frontier models — face heavier duties on top: model evaluations, adversarial testing or red-teaming, reporting serious incidents, and cybersecurity. These GPAI rules applied from the second of August 2025. So even if you only ever build on top of a foundation model, the model itself is now governed beneath you.

1.title: Tier 3 — Transparency Obligations
1.text: Down at the limited-risk tier, the duties are mostly about honesty. Three common cases. Chatbots have to tell people they're interacting with AI, not a human. AI-generated content has to be marked as artificial — deepfakes labeled as such. And emotion-recognition or biometric-categorization systems have to notify the people subject to them. The principle is simple: even when AI is low-risk, people are owed the truth about what they're dealing with. This is the tier where Helios's customer-facing generative assistant lands — so Helios will need to disclose, clearly, that customers are talking to an AI.

1.title: The Timeline (As of Mid-2026)
1.text: Let's lay out the timeline — and remember the currency warning. The Act entered into force in August 2024. In February 2025, the prohibitions and a new AI-literacy duty kicked in. In August 2025, the GPAI rules and the governance structures applied. In August 2026, fine enforcement for GPAI begins, along with some transparency duties. In December 2026, those two new prohibitions arrive. Then the big one: the high-risk obligations under Annex III, which were originally due in August 2026, were postponed by the 2026 "Digital Omnibus" package to December 2027 — and the product-embedded Annex I systems to August 2028. So the high-risk dates moved, and they moved recently. Please confirm the live timeline before you build a compliance plan around any of these.

1.title: Penalties
1.text: What happens if you don't comply? The penalties are deliberately severe — GDPR-scale. For the prohibited practices, fines reach up to thirty-five million euros, or seven percent of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. For most other obligations — high-risk duties, GPAI duties — up to fifteen million or three percent. And for supplying incorrect information to authorities, up to seven and a half million or one percent. These numbers are designed to be felt at board level. The message to organizations is unmistakable: AI non-compliance is not a minor line-item fine, it's a balance-sheet risk.

1.title: Helios Under the EU AI Act
1.text: Let's run Helios through all of this. The hiring tool falls under Annex III employment, so it's high-risk. Helios bought the tool, which makes Helios the deployer and the vendor the provider. So Helios's duties as deployer are: use the system according to the provider's instructions, ensure genuine human oversight of its recommendations, monitor how it performs, keep the logs, run a fundamental-rights impact assessment, and inform affected candidates. And because it's a bought-in tool, Helios must demand the provider's conformity evidence before relying on it. The lesson: being the deployer rather than the builder doesn't take you off the hook. It just puts you on a different hook.

1.title: Don't Forget GDPR — AI Decisions Were Already Regulated
1.text: Before we leave Europe, one essential point people miss: the AI Act did not arrive into an empty room. GDPR — the EU's privacy law — has been regulating AI-driven decisions since 2018. Two pieces matter most. Article 22 gives individuals the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing when it produces legal or similarly significant effects — together with rights to obtain human intervention, to express their view, and to contest the outcome. And the Data Protection Impact Assessment — the DPIA — required for high-risk processing of personal data, is the direct ancestor of the AI Act's fundamental-rights impact assessment. So for Helios's hiring tool, GDPR and the AI Act apply together, not separately. And here's the lesson to carry through the whole course: AI governance always layers on top of existing privacy law — never instead of it.

1.title: Part B — The US: Fragmented & Shifting
1.text: Now Part B: the United States — and I'll present this neutrally, because it's politically live. The headline is that, unlike the EU, the US has no single comprehensive federal AI law. Instead it's a patchwork. At the federal level, a December 2025 executive order pushed for a national AI policy framework intended to preempt state laws seen as inconsistent with it, set up an AI litigation task force, and ordered a review of burdensome state laws. But here's the crucial legal point: an executive order cannot, by itself, overturn state law — only Congress or the courts can do that. So as of mid-2026, this is an unresolved tug-of-war between federal and state power, and in the meantime, state laws remain in force and enforceable. Watch this space, and don't assume the state laws have gone away.

1.title: US State Laws That Bite
1.text: And those state laws genuinely bite — especially on employment AI, which is the most regulated AI use case in the US. The clearest example is New York City's Local Law 144, in force since 2023, which requires annual independent bias audits of automated employment decision tools. Colorado passed the first broad "high-risk AI" law, then delayed it, and ultimately repealed and replaced it with a narrower automated-decision-making statute taking effect in 2027 — a saga that itself tells you how contested this is. And Texas and California both brought AI laws into effect on the first of January, 2026. For Helios, the punchline is direct: its hiring tool almost certainly needs a bias audit to operate in New York City, regardless of what happens at the federal level.

1.title: Part C — UK, Canada & China
1.text: Part C, the rest of the world — three contrasting bets. The UK has chosen a pro-innovation, principles-based path: no single AI law, instead five high-level principles that existing sector regulators interpret, plus an AI Safety Institute focused on frontier-model risks. Canada's proposed AI and Data Act stalled, and the country is rethinking its approach — a reminder that not every effort makes it across the line. And China sits at the other end entirely: among the most prescriptive regimes in the world, with binding rules on recommendation algorithms, on "deep synthesis" — that's synthetic media — and on generative AI, including registration and labeling requirements. Light-touch, in-flux, and tightly controlled — three completely different models, which is why you map obligations market by market.

1.title: The International Layer
1.text: Above all the national law sits an international layer that's quietly pulling toward convergence. The most significant piece is the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on AI, adopted in 2024 — the first binding international treaty on artificial intelligence, anchored in human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. Alongside it, the OECD AI Principles provide the shared values base that, as we saw in Module 3, almost everyone echoes. And the G7's Hiroshima Process offers a voluntary code of conduct for advanced AI, endorsed by dozens of jurisdictions. None of this replaces national law, but it's slowly knitting the fragmented landscape together.

1.title: Operating Across Regimes & Recap
1.text: So how do you operate across all these regimes at once without going mad? The practical strategy is "comply to the highest bar." You build one strong core governance program that meets the strictest requirement you're subject to — usually the EU AI Act — and then you add market-specific pieces on top, like a New York bias audit or a Chinese registration. One robust core, plus local add-ons. Quick recap of this big module: the EU AI Act is risk-based, extraterritorial, phased through 2028, with GDPR-scale fines. The US is fragmented with a contested federal preemption fight. The UK is light-touch, China prescriptive, and the Council of Europe treaty is binding. And always verify the live dates. Next, the frameworks that turn all of this into an actual program — NIST and ISO 42001.
